title: Face Down
logline: A city at night from above, a sea at dawn, a phone face down on a table in the morning. Nobody in frame. One line. The bots worked through the night; you do not have to look.
insight: What people want most from their phone is to need it less. An app that promises that has to be brave enough to never show a screen. We show the night (the work, heard not seen), the dawn (the world turning without you), and the morning (the phone face down, nothing asking for you). The line arrives only when the viewer has already felt it.
treatment:
0.0-6.0 s. SHOT 1, STOCK: a city at night seen from high above, a vertical canyon of lights, traffic as slow points; locked off, or a drift so slow it reads as still (a 16:9 source cropped to 9:16 is fine, the height is the point). Grade: cold, contrast up, saturation down a third, fine grain, light vignette. Nothing on screen, no type, no logo. SOUND: a drone in D, two octaves low, barely moving; a pulse at 40 bpm so soft it is felt in the chest rather than heard; at 2.4 s one bell, far and reverberant (Plan's bell); at 4.0 s a second, a different pitch (Travel's); at 5.4 s a third (Keybot's). They are jobs finishing somewhere in the night. Nobody needs to know that; the frame is enough.

6.0 s. HARD CUT. The pulse stops dead on the cut. This is the first event.

6.0-11.5 s. SHOT 2, STOCK: the sea at dawn, horizon high in the frame (two thirds water), the sun not yet up or just touching the line. If the clip has one small swimmer or one figure on the shore, better; if not, the sea alone is enough. Locked off. Grade: the warmth rises by a hair every second across the shot (the day arriving, done in the grade not the footage). No type. SOUND: surf, far; the drone thins to a single held note; no bells.

11.5 s. HARD CUT.

11.5-18.0 s. SHOT 3, STOCK: a dark wooden table by a window, morning light from the side, a phone lying face down near the window, a cup if the clip has one, no hands, no person. Locked. Grade: warm, soft, with a vignette so the lower half of the frame is dark enough for white type. 13.0-15.0 s: the headline writes on in white in the lower third, heavy Geist, two lines, no full stop: "Your day" (13.0-13.8), then "in good hands" (14.0-15.0) with "hands" in Caveat. 15.2-15.7 s: a brush underline in clay #C9683F drawn left to right under "hands". Hold to 18.0 with nothing else moving but the light. SOUND: the room; one bird outside; at 16.6 s one bell, near this time and clear (the clay bell, the hero's); the drone resolves onto the tonic.

18.0 s. The white paper sheet slides up. Everything cuts to silence except the paper's whisper. Second event.

18.0-22.5 s. END CARD as built: the hero on his bar by his cream gloves (the quiet rhyme with "hands"; we do not point at it), the painted X0 mark drawn in three strokes, "Your team of bots", the hand-drawn stamp "Coming soon / x0bot.com". SOUND: three brush strokes, the final chord, low and warm, the stamp's thud. Out.

Our clips: none used. This film is deliberately empty of our existing material so the manifesto stands on its own frames.

title: Leave at 4:40
logline: A cup of tea by a window, a coat by a door, one small note taped to the frame, and a person who walks, not runs, to a train everyone else in advertising sprints for.
insight: Being on time is not a skill, it is a quiet mind. Every advert shows someone running for a train. The good life is walking to it. Plan does one unglamorous thing here, it tells you when to leave, and we show what that buys: a walk.

title: Who Presses Pay
job: a value (you stay in charge: bots ask before they book, pay or message anyone; you always press pay)
logline: A fox in a library, filmed like an interview, asks the one question everybody asks about a bot that books things. The lights go out. Two words.
insight: People do not fear that a machine will fail them. They fear it will act without asking. Trust is not cleverness; it is the pause before the payment. So we let a sceptic ask, and we answer with the fewest words we have.
treatment:
0.0-5.5 s. OUR CLIP 3 (its first 5.5 s of 7.3): the fox in the cream cable-knit sweater in the leather armchair, the wood-panelled library, talking and gesturing to camera. We treat it as a filmed interview: ink letterbox bars top and bottom (a 4:5 window inside the 9:16), grade darker and warmer, contrast up, a vignette so the fox sits in a pool of candle-coloured light and the shelves fall away, fine grain. He speaks (neural voice-over, Indian English male, older, measured, dry, unhurried: a Delhi professor who has seen things; slowed a little, pitched down a little; mixed close and dry like an interview mic, not a dub): 0.6 s "It finds the flight." 1.6 s "It finds the hotel." 2.8 s "And who presses pay?" (ends about 4.0 s). Only the last sentence is written as he says it: Caveat, white, lower third just above the bottom bar, word by word on his word times, "And who presses pay?" (2.8-4.0). 4.0-5.5 s: silence. He keeps gesturing, as the clip does; it reads as waiting for an answer. We hold. SOUND: the room, close and dry (wood, no echo), no music, his voice, a pen scratch under the handwriting, then the silence, which is the content.

5.5 s. HARD CUT TO INK BLACK, the event, with one short low boom and nothing after it.

5.5-9.5 s. BLACK, full frame #0A0A0A, no bars. 5.6 s: "You do" slams in, white, heavy Geist, centred, one line. 6.4-7.2 s: under it, "always" written in Caveat in clay #C9683F. 7.2-7.7 s: a brush underline in clay under "always". 8.0-8.8 s: below, small, Geist regular, white, one line (it may wrap to two): "Bots ask before they book, pay or message anyone". Hold to 9.5. SOUND: a single low sustained note begins at 5.6 s (the drone's tonic) and nothing else.

9.5 s. HARD CUT.

title: The Sceptic
job: a value (you stay in charge: bots ask before they book, pay or message anyone; you always press pay)
logline: A deadpan documentary interview with a fox who does not trust bots, and who, question by question, describes exactly how ours behave.
insight: Nobody wants to trust software with their money or their mother. They want to not have to. A thing that always asks first needs no trust at all, only a thumb. The sceptic is not converted; he is simply, grudgingly, correct.
treatment:
FRAME (whole film). 1080x1920 white paper. A centred window 960x1200 (a 4:5 opening) from y=240 to y=1440 with a hairline dip-pen ink frame. CLIP 3 is scaled and cropped into it so the fox's eyes sit on the vertical centre line and his head in the upper third; the library behind him (books, globe, brass candelabra) frames him symmetrically. Light grain, a soft vignette inside the window only, warmth up a touch. Top band (y 0 to 240): small letterspaced ink caps, centred: A SHORT INTERVIEW WITH A SCEPTIC. Bottom band (y 1440 to 1920): the transcript, ink Geist medium 46 px, centred, typed word by word on the voice's word times with a blinking ink cursor. Questions are never heard: each is a paper card that HARD CUTS into the window (no animation, no slide), the question set in heavy ink Geist, two lines, centred; the transcript band clears to the single letter Q. The camera never moves. Nothing in the frame moves but the fox and the type. The clock ticks.

0.0-1.4 COLD OPEN. The window holds a STILL of the fox (CLIP 3, frame at about 0.3 s): a fox in a cream cable-knit sweater in a leather armchair, hands folded mid-gesture, looking straight at us. Top band label is already there. The transcript types: Subject: a fox. Position: unconvinced. Sound: library room tone, a clock at 60 bpm.

1.4-2.5 Q1 CARD. Hard cut, window to paper. Heavy ink: Would you let a bot / plan your trip? One soft bell. Transcript: Q.

2.5-4.0 A1. Hard cut back: the fox alive (CLIP 3, 1.4-2.9), one open palm. He says: It can find one. Transcript types the words as he says them.

4.0-5.1 Q2 CARD. And pay for it? Bell.

5.1-7.2 A2. Fox (CLIP 3, 2.9-5.0), his larger gesture. No. I press pay. Myself. Transcript types. Builders slide the segment by up to half a second so the biggest hand movement lands on Myself.

7.2-8.4 EXHIBIT A. Hard cut, window to paper. Centred: a round button drawn with a dip pen, slightly wobbly, the word Pay inside in heavy ink. Beneath it, small typed ink, two lines: Exhibit A. The button. / Pressed by: you. A clay (#C9683F) brush tick under the word you. Clock ticks. No voice.

8.4-9.5 Q3 CARD. Would you let it / message your mother? Bell.

9.5-12.0 A3. Fox (CLIP 3, 5.0-7.3, then hold the last frame 0.2 s). It asks first. A half-second beat. Then I say no. Transcript types with the beat kept.

12.0-13.1 Q4 CARD. What does it do / with your data? Bell.

13.1-14.9 A4. Fox (CLIP 3, 0.4-2.2, a stretch far enough from the cold open that the gesture reads as new). It does not sell it. I checked. Transcript types.

14.9-16.0 Q5 CARD. So you trust it? Bell.

16.0-17.3 A5. Fox (CLIP 3, 2.0-3.3). I don't have to. Transcript types.

17.3-18.6 THE FREEZE. The fox freezes mid-gesture, one hand up. The clock stops. Room tone only. The grade cools by a hair (the freeze that goes cold). Nothing happens for 1.3 s. Only the cursor blinks.

The word ask is handwritten in Caveat and a clay brush underline paints beneath it left to right over 0.4 s. The transcript band clears and types: End of interview. A warm chord swells under.

title: A Trip in Six Chapters
logline: A weekend by the sea told as six numbered chapters: five of them kept by Travel, the sixth kept, pointedly, for you.
insight: A trip is twenty tabs and one thumb. People do not mind the thumb; they mind the tabs. Show the tabs as tidy chapters with pictures, and the thumb as the only chapter with no picture at all, and you have said what Travel does and what it will never do in the same breath.
treatment:
FRAME (whole film). Footage sits full-bleed inside a 36 px white paper mount with a hairline ink dip-pen rule (a mounted photograph). Every shot is chosen or cropped so its subject is dead centre and level. title: Great at One Thing

logline: A deadpan census of people who are great at one thing, ending on a man who is great at dinner and less great at everything after it, and the team that takes the rest.
insight: Nobody is great at everything, and the people we admire never tried to be. The relief of a team is not that it does your life for you; it is that you get to keep the one thing you are actually good at, and hand off the rest without apology.

title: Count-In
logline: A whole day as a drum part: sixteen small jobs cut on the beat, doubling in speed until the words pile into a black scrawl, then silence, and the hero bot swings in and sweeps it clean.
insight: Nobody's day is hard because of one big thing. It is hard because it is a beat you did not choose and cannot drop: tea, keys, train, mail, call, milk, pick-up, bins, bills, sleep. You are always a half-beat behind. What people want is not more time; it is for someone else to hold the rhythm for a while.
treatment:
TEMPO 120 bpm. Beat = 0.50 s = 15 frames. Bar = 2.00 s. Grade on all footage: warm, desaturated 30%, light grain, soft vignette, so sixteen clips from five sources read as one world.

0.00-2.00 BAR 1, THE COUNT. Stock: an alarm clock, close, second hand moving (search "alarm clock close up ticking", fallback "analog clock second hand macro"). Locked off. On each beat (0.00, 0.50, 1.00, 1.50) a hat click, and a small white Caveat numeral writes itself beside the clock: "1", "2", "3", "4". The "4" is bigger and its ink bleeds.

2.00 DOWNBEAT. The alarm rings (synth bell rattle, two beats) and we CUT. From here every cut is a drum hit: kick on beats 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, hats on eighths. Every cut lands with ONE white heavy Geist word slammed centre (scale 1.15 to 1.00 in 3 frames): a job of the day. The word lives only as long as its shot.

2.00-6.00 BARS 2-3, QUARTER NOTES. 8 shots x 0.50 s (15 frames each):
2.00 kettle boiling, steam (search "kettle boiling steam close up") - word: tea
2.50 toothbrush under a running tap ("brushing teeth sink close up") - brush
3.00 a hand grabs keys off a table ("picking up keys from table") - keys
3.50 a front door closing ("front door closing") - go
4.00 metro doors closing ("metro train doors closing", "subway doors close") - train
4.50 hands typing on a laptop ("typing laptop keyboard close up") - mail
5.00 a phone buzzing face down on a table ("phone vibrating on table") - call
5.50 a wall calendar page ("wall calendar flipping pages") - dentist

6.00-10.00 BARS 4-5, EIGHTH NOTES. 16 shots x 0.25 s (alternate 8 and 7 frames to hold tempo). Hats double. The words land faster and start to crowd: each new word slams slightly off-centre and the previous ones no longer clear fully, they drop to 40% and stay.
6.00 crowded market ("crowded market street", "busy bazaar") - milk
6.25 grocery bag dropped on a counter ("grocery bag kitchen counter") - bread
6.50 a child asleep in a car seat ("child sleeping car seat") - pick-up
6.75 a bus in rain, city night ("bus in rain city night") - late
7.00 rain on a window ("rain on window") - umbrella

7.50 phone face down (reuse) - mum
7.75 calendar (reuse) - Friday
8.00 OUR CLIP 1: the man cooking at night, back to camera, steam under the hood light, a 0.25 s sliver from its middle - dinner
8.25 a dog waiting at a door ("dog waiting at door") - walk
8.50 kettle (reuse) - tea

9.00 door (reuse) - bins
9.25 metro doors (reuse) - tickets

9.75 a bedside lamp switched off ("bedside lamp switch off night") - sleep

10.00-12.00 BAR 6, SIXTEENTH NOTES. The same 16 shots in the same order, 0.125 s each (frame pattern 4,4,4,3 repeating to hold 120 bpm), each sliver speed-ramped 2x inside itself. The words no longer clear at all: all sixteen slam on top of one another into a white stack, and on every hit the stack jitters one frame left or right. Snare roll under it, a riser, the grade heats (warmth and contrast up), the vignette tightens. Keep luminance deltas between slivers moderate; the rhythm is in the motion and the words, not in flashing.

12.00 FREEZE. The last sixteenth is the ALARM CLOCK from 0.00, mid-ring: the day ends where it began. Hard freeze on it. Sound cuts to nothing but a thin room tone. Over 10 frames the frame goes cold: full desaturation, lifted to a pale photocopy grey, and the stacked white words invert to ink #0A0A0A, so the pile now reads as a black scrawl over a grey clock. Hold, nothing moves, to 12.50.

12.50-14.50 THE HERO. From the top edge the hero bot swings down into frame on his clay bar (#C9683F), upside down, hanging by his cream gloves, a pendulum that settles in two swings (a wooden creak, then one tiny bell). His two cream eyes look down at the scrawl. One blink at 13.80.

14.50-15.50 THE SWEEP. One glove lets go of the bar and flicks (or the launch move, if it reads as a sweep). The scrawl loosens into paper scraps and slides off the bottom of frame (paper rustle), and the grey clock frame wipes down with it, leaving plain white cotton paper. The hero stays hanging top of frame and re-grips.

15.50-19.50 HEADLINE, ink on paper, heavy Geist, two lines, no full stop:
15.50 "All that noise" slams (a muted kick)
16.50 "One quiet team" slams (a softer kick); "quiet" is Caveat handwriting, written over 12 frames
17.20 a brush underline in clay #C9683F draws under "quiet" (brush swish)
Hold. At 18.80 the hero's eyes move from the headline to camera.

19.50-24.00 END CARD (fixed, 4.5 s). The white paper sheet slides up beneath the hero, who re-settles on his bar. The painted X0 mark is drawn in three strokes on the beat (20.00, 20.50, 21.00: three low taps). "Your team of bots". The hand-drawn stamp "Coming soon / x0bot.com" thuds at 23.00. The final chord opens at 20.00 and sustains. The hero winks at 22.50.

why_it_works_mute: The numerals 1-2-3-4 beside a clock promise a count even in silence. Then the eye gets a drum part: a hard cut and one big word every half second, then every quarter second, then a flicker, each word a job you recognise from your own day. The words literally pile up into a black scrawl; you feel the overload before you read anything. The freeze going cold is a visible rest. A painted bot swings in over the frozen frame, looks at the mess, flicks it off the page. Then four words. The whole arc, overload to relief, is in the motion and the type; the sound is a bonus.
risk: Sixteen clips from four licence sources will not match; the single grade, the grain and the one-word system have to carry the unity, so test the grade on the ugliest clip first. Eight cuts a second for two seconds is a flicker: keep luminance deltas small and let the motion, not brightness, make the rhythm. If fewer shots are found, repeat more; it still works at eight unique shots. The freeze-goes-cold is a campaign device already used twice; here the departure is that the hero physically arrives over real footage, so the builders must sell the swing and the sweep or the ending will look like the template.
director: RHYTHM. I cut on the beat and let sound be the drummer; when the sound is off, the cut still is the drummer. Three spots, three tempos. COUNT-IN is a drum kit made of ordinary objects at 120 bpm, doubling until it breaks, then a rest, then the hero. ONE PLACE is five tempos at once that lock into one on a downbeat, for the Travel bot. THE SCEPTIC is a comic accelerando: a fox interviewee cut off by taped cards that answer faster each time, for the value "you stay in charge". Shared grammar across all three: the cut is a drum hit, the freeze is a rest, type lands like a snare, the hero is a physical presence over real footage, and every film ends on the fixed end card. Everything here is buildable from the three clips we own, generic open-licence shots, the synth kit, paper components and edge-tts.

title: One Place
logline: Five strips of a trip, each pulsing at its own tempo, fight for the frame until a single downbeat slams them into one paper card that writes the whole trip, and you press pay.
insight: A trip is not hard to take; it is hard to hold. Dates live in one head, tickets in a mailbox, weather on a screen, the room in a thread, packing on a scrap of paper, and each of them has its own clock. The relief people want is not a cheaper trip. It is one sheet.
treatment:
Travel bot colour: sea #3E6E8E. Frame divided into five horizontal strips of 1080 x 384 for the first six seconds.

0.00-0.20 white cotton paper, silent.

0.20 STRIP 1 wipes in from the left into the top fifth: calendar pages flipping (search "calendar pages flipping close up", "flip calendar"). 1.40 STRIP 3, third fifth: storm clouds in timelapse (search "storm clouds timelapse", fallback "rain on window"). KICK C at 120 bpm. 1.70 label "weather".
2.00 STRIP 4, fourth fifth: a hotel corridor, or a key slid across a reception desk (search "hotel corridor", "hotel key reception desk"). KICK D at 136 bpm. 2.30 label "stays".
2.60 STRIP 5, bottom fifth: hands cramming clothes into a suitcase (search "packing suitcase hands close up"). KICK E at 152 bpm, highest. 2.90 label "packing".

3.20-6.00 FIVE TEMPOS AT ONCE. Five kicks at five speeds that never agree; each strip jumps only on its own hit, so the frame is a stack of five metronomes out of phase. From 4.00 the strips also slide horizontally against each other, alternating directions, a slot machine that will not stop; the labels shiver one frame on each hit; the hairline gaps between strips flicker white paper. Riser from 4.00. Contrast climbs. Saturation is pulled down everywhere except a cool cast in the shadows.

6.00 DOWNBEAT. One boom. All five kicks stop dead. The five strips slam toward the centre and collapse into a single white paper card, the taped card, tape ripping on at two corners (tape rip SFX, 2 frames each). THE CARD WRITES ITSELF, Caveat in ink, one line per bell (Travel's bell), each line written in about 14 frames:

title: Pahunch gaye?
logline: Every Indian journey ends with the same two-word message. A film of arrivals, one question written over each, and two paper cards that quietly show who got them there.
insight: In India, 'I love you' is sent as 'Pahunch gaye?' (Reached?). Love here is logistics: the family runs on arrivals, and someone is always waiting for the haan. A team of bots that handles the leaving-time and the tickets is, in the end, in the business of letting you say yes.

title: Uncle is right
job: a value (you stay in charge: you always press pay)
logline: A retired professor who happens to be a fox, interviewed in his study, says the one thing every Indian family's sceptic says about machines and money. The brand stops the film and agrees with him on paper.
insight: Every Indian family has an uncle who trusts no machine with money, and he has usually been right. Trust is not won by promising; it is won by leaving your hand on the wallet. 'You always press pay' is that uncle's rule, made into a product, and the most honest thing a bot company can say to him is: sahi hai.
treatment:
FORMAT: 9:16, 1080x1920, 30 fps, 22 s. Thin ink letterbox bars, a documentary grade (blacks lifted a touch, fine grain). Grammar: what the fox says is white Caveat handwriting on his word times, subtitle position; what the bots say is ink type on paper. Clip 3 (7.3 s) is cut into two takes: TAKE A = clip 0.0-3.8, TAKE B = clip 3.8-7.3.

0.0-3.8 CLIP 3 TAKE A: the fox in the cream cable-knit sweater in the leather armchair, the wood-panelled library warm behind him, talking and gesturing to camera. At 0.3 a lower-third fades in bottom-left, small white Geist with a thin clay rule above it: 'Prof. Lomri (retd.)' / 'Keeps his own wallet'. Sound: a clock at 60 bpm (the pulse), a wood-room tone. At 0.4 his voice (neural Indian English male, en-IN-PrabhatNeural, rate -10%, measured, an elder's cadence, never comic): 'Bots? Theek hai. Let them find my train. But paisa?' Each word appears in white Caveat under the lower-third region on his word times, like a dubbed interview.

3.8-9.0 FREEZE on the clearest raised-hand frame nearest 3.8 (the builders pick the frame and fit the voice so 'paisa?' lands on it). The frame goes cold: saturation down a third, cooler, grain up; the clock stops; a drone only. At 4.2 the hero bot swings down from the top edge, hanging by his cream gloves from his clay bar, big cream eyes; his eyes slide to the fox, then to us, and he nods slowly, upside down. At 5.2 a tape rip: a white paper card tapes onto the frozen frame beside the fox's hand. Top of card: Travel's dotted head and 'Travel' in sea #3E6E8E. Ink Geist: 'Pune, Fri 17:40' / 'Coach S6, seat 23'. Below that a hand-drawn button outline with 'Pay' inside it, and under the button in small ink: 'only you press this'. At 7.2 a line writes on in ink across the frame below the card: 'Bots ask before they book, pay or message anyone.' A sea bell.

9.0-12.5 UNFREEZE into CLIP 3 TAKE B: colour returns, the clock resumes. The fox gestures and settles. Voice at 9.3: 'Hmm.' A pause. At 10.8: 'Sahi hai.' Handwritten subtitles on word times. The hero bot, still hanging at the top, blinks once on 'Sahi hai'.

12.5-17.5 FREEZE on the last frame of take B, and this freeze stays WARM (saturation kept, warmth up one notch): the freeze that does not go cold, because he agreed. The hero bot lifts out of the top of frame (the launch move). Headline writes on in white heavy Geist, two lines, no full stop: 'Uncle is right' / 'You always press pay', with 'pay' in white Caveat and a brush underline in icon clay #C9683F. Small white line below: 'Nothing is booked, paid or sent till you say yes'. The clock keeps ticking under a warm chord.

17.5-22.0 END CARD (fixed, 4.5 s): the white paper sheet slides up, the hero on his bar, the X0 mark drawn in three strokes, 'Your team of bots', the stamp 'Coming soon / x0bot.com'.

director: The Humanist. In the lineage of Zoya Akhtar and Satyajit Ray: the everyday India of kitchens, trains, phones and the two-word message; Hinglish exactly as it is spoken, fillers and all; the small observed gesture over the big idea; dignity first, and the smile a viewer recognises from their own house. Three spots, three jobs, three different devices, one grammar shared with the campaign: what a person SAYS is handwriting (Caveat, white on film), what gets SETTLED is type (Geist), a bot's work arrives on paper, and a person always has the last word. Spot 1 is a refrain film built on the question every Indian family sends ("Pahunch gaye?"); Spot 2 gives Keybot a mother in Jaipur and a son in Bengaluru, one minute apart; Spot 3 finally gives the fox his voice as the family's sceptic uncle, and lets the brand agree with him.

title: He had a team
job: manifesto (awareness): the whole idea, a team of bots, each great at one thing, now for anyone
logline: Through a hole torn in white paper we watch old films of the office that once ran one man's life; a painted bot hangs in every room and a card names the bot that does that job now. He had a team. Now you do.
insight: Having someone was always the luxury. The person with a team got their life back while everyone else carried their own day in their head. People do not want a smarter phone; they want a someone.
treatment:
FORMAT 9:16, 24 s. The whole film happens on a sheet of white cotton paper; the real world is an old film seen through a hole torn in it.

0.0-1.2 WHITE PAPER, full frame, faint grain. A tear opens from the centre (rough-edged mask wipe, 0.6 s, paper-tear sound) into a 4:3 window sitting a little below centre (window height about 55% of frame, paper margins above and below). Inside: black-and-white archive film with its own scratches and flicker kept, graded to the brand greys (no sepia), light vignette.

1.2-3.8 ARCHIVE A (Internet Archive / Prelinger, public domain): an executive at a desk dictating; a stenographer writes on a pad. Hold frames to slow it about 10%. At 1.4 the hero bot's two cream gloves grab the torn top edge of the window and he swings down into the old film, upside down, hanging inside the room (soft knock). Big cream eyes blink once, then follow the pencil. At 2.6 a white paper card is TAPED into the paper margin just under the stenographer, like a museum label (tape slap): Keybot's dotted head in clay #A9573A, 'Keybot' in heavy Geist ink. VO 1.4-3.4: 'He had someone to write it down.'

3.8-6.2 ARCHIVE B: a desk appointment book, a hand writing a name into a time slot, a wall clock. HARD CUT inside the window only; the paper and the hanging hero do not cut (he is the one constant; the room changes behind him). His eyes track the hand. Card taped at 5.0: Plan's dotted head ochre #8F6A1F, 'Plan'. VO 4.0-5.6: 'Someone to keep his day.'

6.2-8.8 ARCHIVE C: a railway ticket window, or a porter with suitcases, or a passenger train pulling out of a platform. The hero's eyes go wide at the train. Card at 7.5: Travel's dotted head sea #3E6E8E, 'Travel'. VO 6.4-8.0: 'Someone to book his train.'

8.8-11.2 ARCHIVE D: a boardroom, men round a table, one of them writing the minutes. Card at 9.8: an ink dotted head, 'Notes'. VO 9.0-10.6: 'Someone to take the notes.'

11.2-13.8 ARCHIVE E: a telephone switchboard operator plugging cords. Card at 12.4: five small dotted heads in a row (clay, ochre, sea, moss, ink), 'Ask any bot'. VO 11.3-13.6: 'And someone to put him through to the right one.'

13.8-15.5 FREEZE on the operator mid-plug. The window goes cold (full desaturate, vignette deepens, flicker stops). Silence but for a thin drone. The hero turns his eyes slowly to camera.

15.5-19.0 HEADLINE on the white paper above the window, ink, heavy Geist, two lines, no full stop: 'He had a team' slams at 15.7 (boom); 'Now you do' slams at 16.6 (boom). 19.0-19.5 The hero lets go of the torn edge (the launch move) and drops out of the bottom of frame (whoosh).

title: Whisper
job: a bot (Keybot): filler out, punctuation in, names kept; Hindi and Hinglish first
logline: A mother whispers a Hinglish message over a sleeping child; her umms peel out of the sentence like stickers, the punctuation stamps in, the name stays, and the line leaves clean.
insight: The moments we most need to send a message are the moments we cannot type, and nobody speaks in sentences; we whisper in umms and half-words and are a little ashamed of how that looks written down. Being written cleanly feels like being understood.
treatment:
FORMAT 9:16, 22 s. One real clip, a whisper, and a bot who tidies what she said.

0.0-1.5 STOCK: the back seat of a car at night; a small child asleep in a car seat, head tipped; streetlights slide across the face. Cool grade, fine grain, slight vignette. Sound: engine hum; a turn-signal tick that becomes the pulse of the spot (synth click, 72 bpm, soft).

1.5-7.0 A WHISPER (neural Indian English female, low, slow, Hinglish). Her words appear across the lower third in white Caveat handwriting, word by word on her word times, exactly as spoken, wrapping to three lines:
'Umm, Mummy, hum nine tak aa jayenge,'
'uh, haan...'
'aur Aarav so gaya'
The footage keeps moving. No freeze (we leave the cold freeze to the other films).

7.0-8.0 From the top edge of frame two cream gloves grip (as if the car's grab handle) and the hero bot swings down upside down into the car, flat painted black against the real dark. His eyes land on the sentence; one blink (a tiny vinyl squeak).

8.0-11.0 He flicks the mess off. At 8.2 his glove flicks 'Umm,': it peels like a sticker (crisp paper peel), tumbles, and drops out of the bottom of frame (a tiny paper landing in the footwell). 9.0: 'uh,' peels and falls. 9.8: 'haan...' peels and falls. The child sleeps through it.

11.0-12.5 The remaining words slide together to close the gaps (paper slide). Punctuation is stamped in with tiny ink thuds: a comma after 'Mummy' (11.3), a full stop after 'jayenge' (11.7), a capital A on 'Aur' and a full stop after 'gaya' (12.0). At 12.2 a short brush underline in Keybot's clay #A9573A paints under 'Aarav': the name kept. The line now reads, still handwritten: 'Mummy, hum nine tak aa jayenge. Aur Aarav so gaya.'

12.5-13.3 In one frame the handwriting snaps to clean white Geist type (the campaign's device), Keybot's small clay dotted head at the end of the line.

13.3-14.3 The hero nods once. The typed line slides up and out of frame as if sent; a single soft Keybot bell. He looks at the sleeping child, then at us.

14.3-17.5 HEADLINE, white on the footage, heavy Geist, two lines, no full stop: 'Say it messy' slams at 14.5; 'It writes it clean' slams at 15.3. 'messy' is in Caveat; the clay brush underline paints 15.6-16.1. Small white Geist beneath at 16.3: 'Keybot. Any app. 50+ languages.' Hold.

17.5-22.0 END CARD (fixed, 4.5 s): white paper slides up, the hero on his bar, the X0 mark in three strokes, 'Your team of bots', stamp 'Coming soon / x0bot.com'. Final chord, soft.

title: Nobody asks a fox
job: a value (you stay in charge: bots ask before they book or pay; you always press pay)
logline: A fox in a cardigan recounts, to camera, the day a machine found his train and then stopped and asked him. He pressed pay himself. Nobody asks a fox.
insight: Being asked is a form of respect. We trust the helper who stops at the money and looks at us. The sly fox is disarmed not by cleverness but by manners.
treatment:
FORMAT 9:16, 20 s. A fox is interviewed about the day a machine asked his permission. CLIP 3 (7.3 s) is used in full, in two runs with a freeze between them; no stock.

0.0-0.6 WHITE PAPER. A dip-pen frame draws itself just inside the edges (0.5 s, nib scratch). Inside it CLIP 3 fades up: the fox in the cream sweater, leather armchair, the library's warm light. Grade: keep the wood warm but pull saturation about 15% so the sea and clay read. Fine grain.

0.6-3.6 CLIP 3 run 1 (clip 0.0-3.0 at 1.0x). A taped paper scrap, lower left, small ink Geist: 'A fox' / 'Client since Friday'. He is dubbed: a neural UK English male, dry, unhurried, a don being interviewed. His words appear as white Caveat handwriting word by word in the lower third. VO 0.8-2.4: 'It found the train. The six-ten.' VO 2.7-3.5: 'Then it stopped.' He gestures as he talks; the lips will not match and we do not pretend they do. This is a dubbed documentary.

3.6-4.4 FREEZE on the frame where his paw is raised toward camera (the builders pick the frame whose next ten frames carry the paw forward). The frame goes a touch cold. Room tone only; a clock ticks at 60 bpm.

4.4-6.2 A white paper card is TAPED onto the frozen frame (tape slap), positioned exactly where the paw will land: Travel's dotted head in sea #3E6E8E at the top, then in ink Geist 'Fri 6:10 pm train' / 'Book and pay?' and two hand-drawn buttons: 'Pay' (sea fill, white type) and 'Not now' (ink outline). At 5.0 a soft Travel bell. Hold. Nobody moves.

6.2-6.6 UNFREEZE (clip 3.0-3.4). His real gesture completes and his paw arrives on 'Pay': the in-camera trick, the card placed to the clip's own motion. 'Pay' depresses for two frames; a clay stamp slams onto the card: 'Booked' (stamp thud).

6.6-11.5 CLIP 3 run 2 (clip 3.4-7.3 at 1.0x, then hold the last frame 1.0 s). The card stays taped to the frame, one corner lifting as he talks. VO 6.5-7.2: 'It asked me.' VO 7.6-8.5: 'I pressed pay.' Pause. VO 9.4-10.8: 'Nobody asks a fox.' Each line handwritten word by word in white. Hold on his face.

11.5-12.4 From the top edge two cream gloves grip the dip-pen frame and the hero bot lowers in, upside down, looks at the fox, then at us. One wink.

12.4-15.5 FREEZE the fox (cold). HEADLINE, white on footage, heavy Geist, two lines, no full stop: 'It asks first' slams at 12.6; 'You press pay' slams at 13.4. 'asks' is in Caveat; a brush underline in the icon's clay #C9683F paints 13.7-14.2. Small white Geist beneath at 14.4: 'It asks before it books, pays or messages anyone'. Hold.

15.5-20.0 END CARD (fixed, 4.5 s): white paper slides up, the hero on his bar, the X0 mark in three strokes, 'Your team of bots', stamp 'Coming soon / x0bot.com'. Final chord.

title: The Witness
job: manifesto (awareness): what X0 Bot is, defined by what it refuses to do
logline: A fox is cross-examined about his bots. He answers in as few words as possible and wins the room with what they will not do.
insight: Nobody believes a brand describing itself; everybody leans in when someone is made to answer for it under pressure. And the real fear about bots is not that they fail but that they act. So the product is best introduced by a witness who lists what it does and then, under hostile questioning, what it did without him: nothing.
treatment:
FORMAT: 9:16, 30.0 s = film 25.5 s + fixed end card 4.5 s. Two visual registers only, hard-cut against each other for the whole film.

REGISTER 1, THE QUESTION: pure black frame; a small grey "Q" above a question in white heavy Geist, left-aligned in the lower third, two lines max. Each question slams in within one frame with a soft typewriter-carriage click. The questioner is never seen and never heard.

REGISTER 2, THE WITNESS: CLIP 3 (the fox in the library armchair), regraded as a deposition tape: saturation -30%, contrast +20%, blacks crushed so the panelling, books and globes go to ink, the candelabra's warmth kept only in the highlights on his face and sweater, heavy vignette, fine grain. A tiny grey running timecode sits top-left (00:41:07 style) during every witness shot, like a recording. His answers appear beneath his chest as white Caveat handwriting, word by word on the voice's word times (campaign device: handwriting is the human's words; type is the machine's). Voice: en-GB male (edge-tts en-GB-RyanNeural), slow, dry, slightly bored, small room reverb. Clip 3 is 7.3 s and we need 16.5 s of him, so we treat it as a locked deposition camera and re-use it at three punch-ins (100%, 108%, 115%) and two speeds (1.0x, 0.5-0.75x), with freezes covering his silences. Segments are listed per shot.

0.0-0.6  Black. A tape-start click, then thin hiss. A wall clock begins at 60 bpm and never stops until the end card.
